title: Russia Now Supplies More Than Half of India's Oil. Washington Says the Waiver That Made It Possible Is Over.
excerpt: Record Russian crude imports hit 2.66 million barrels a day in June while Iran's petroleum minister lands in Delhi with a rival offer — and the US signals both doors could close.
body:
For the first time on record, more than half of every barrel of crude oil landing at Indian ports comes from Russia. Data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows that Russian crude arrivals averaged 2.66 million barrels per day in the first three weeks of June — a record high — lifting Moscow's share of India's total oil imports to 53.5 per cent.

The number would have been unthinkable four years ago. Before the US-Iran war erupted in late February, Russia accounted for about 23 per cent of India's crude purchases. The Strait of Hormuz blockade, which cut off flows from the Gulf producers India had relied on for decades, forced refiners to scramble for alternatives. Russian barrels, sold at discounts of $4–5 below the global Brent benchmark, became the obvious lifeline.

## Washington Opened the Tap — and Now Wants It Shut

The surge was made possible by a series of US sanctions waivers. Beginning in March, the Trump administration temporarily de-sanctioned Russian oil loaded on tankers, explicitly to ease the worst supply disruption in oil-market history. The waiver was renewed three times, most recently on May 17 for one month.

It expired on June 17. The Treasury did not renew it.

But tankers loaded before the cutoff are still arriving, and Indian refiners — who had locked in purchases weeks in advance — are taking delivery of what they bought legally under the waiver window. The practical effect: record Russian volumes hitting Indian ports even after the formal waiver has lapsed.



> **""We would like to end it as soon as we possibly can because the underlying policy of this country has been to sanction their oil," Rubio told the Senate Foreign Policy Committee earlier this month."**


US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking during a visit to Bahrain, signalled that the door is closing for good. "We would like to end it as soon as we possibly can because the underlying policy of this country has been to sanction their oil," Rubio told the Senate Foreign Policy Committee earlier this month. He described the waivers as "time-limited" measures tied to the supply crisis — not a permanent arrangement.

The final call rests with President Trump, and Rubio noted the decision will be "calibrated to avoid triggering a sharp rise in global oil prices." With Brent now back at $72–73 a barrel — roughly where it traded before the Iran war — Washington has more room to tighten.

## Iran Simultaneously Comes Knocking

The timing is complicated by a second, simultaneous shift. Washington's 60-day sanctions waiver on Iranian energy products, issued on June 23 as part of the nascent US-Iran peace deal, has reopened a door that India closed in 2019.

The National Iranian Oil Company and middlemen based in Singapore and Dubai have approached Indian refiners directly, offering crude at $3–4 per barrel below comparable regional grades. Iranian Petroleum Minister Mohsen Paknejad flew to New Delhi this week for the 11th BRICS Energy Ministers' Meeting and held bilateral talks with India's Oil Minister Hardeep Puri on strengthening hydrocarbon cooperation.

But Indian refiners say they have limited appetite right now. "Most oil companies are covered till August," a source at one refinery told Reuters. "We were not expecting a waiver and had already bought whatever was available in the market." Payment mechanisms and banking channels for Iranian trade remain murky — India's last two Iranian cargoes, received in April, were settled in Chinese yuan — and compliance teams are wary of a waiver that could vanish in 60 days.

## The Dependency Dilemma

India's energy map has been redrawn in four months. Saudi Arabia, India's dominant supplier for years, now ships just 384,000 barrels per day, down from 832,000 before the war. The UAE — the second-largest supplier in June — routes most of its oil through the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline that bypasses the Strait entirely.

If Washington enforces the end of Russian waivers and the Iran window proves too narrow to fill the gap, India faces a difficult repositioning. Middle Eastern term suppliers are already pressuring buyers to honour annual contractual commitments — supply that Indian refiners sidelined when Russian discounts made them the cheaper option.

The RBI, meanwhile, has been burning through reserves defending the rupee, selling a net $8.94 billion in the forex market in April alone. A return to pricier Middle Eastern supply at a time when the rupee sits near 94.4 per dollar would widen the current account deficit and put fresh pressure on the currency.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For the 30 million Indians living abroad, the oil dependency story matters in ways that go beyond barrel counts. A weaker rupee erodes the purchasing power of family remittances; higher energy costs feed through to everything from airfares to food prices; and the geopolitical friction that comes with buying half your oil from a sanctioned supplier complicates the India-US relationship at a moment when a trade deal is tantalisingly close.

India's oil minister struck a diplomatic tone after his meeting with Iran's Paknejad: "India remains committed to enhancing energy security via dialogue, partnership, and a mutually beneficial engagement." The language is careful. The stakes are not.
